docs.title: MPFS Explorer
docs.text: A PureScript browser application for exploring MPFS facts and verifying Cardano transactions without trusting the off-chain service.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Fact exploration — browse token facts with schema-driven rendering, verified end-to-end via Merkle proofs
  2. Untrusted transaction verification — decode unsigned transactions in MPFS semantics so users never blindly sign
  3. Fully off-chain verification — prove fact existence without a Cardano node, using institutional UTXO Merkle roots

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: • Design — architecture, trust model, UX flows

docs.title: UI/UX Evaluation: cardano-mpfs-browser SPA
docs.text: Evidence used: /tmp/uieval/brief.md, src/MPFS/App/View.purs, src/App.purs, src/MPFS/App/Facts.purs, src/MPFS/Client*.purs, src/MPFS/Cage/Wasm.purs, dist/index.html, screenshots /code/moog/final-connect.png, /code/moog/final-tokens.png, /code/moog/final-facts.png, and sibling references in purescript-spa-kit/mui, cardano-mpfs-offchain-ui-redesign/mpfs-spa, cquisitor, and cardano-ledger-inspector. No browser MCP was available.

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text:
• The current SPA is functionally wired but visually still a placeholder. It uses one generic two-column panel for every workflow, so token/fact/request management has weak hierarchy and poor action guidance.
  • The operator's overflow complaint is confirmed. In final-facts.png, request values sprawl far beyond the panel and screenshot width because request/fact rows render raw hex in unbounded flex spans.
  • Requests are the largest UX failure. The UI shows operation/key/value/phase only; it does not clearly show requester, request id, age/deadlines, proof coverage, or who may retract.
  • Hash/key/value handling needs a first-class component: show xxxx…yyyy, keep full value in tooltip/title/detail, and provide one-click copy with copied feedback.
  • Recommendation: choose path A. Keep Halogen and implement the house Material design language with Halogen components plus plain CSS. Do not adopt react-basic+MUI for this asset-managing app.
  • Use the redesigned mpfs-spa and purescript-spa-kit/mui as design/behavior references, not as runtime dependencies. The current app has 1 runtime npm package; the MUI sibling has 86.

Overflow/clipping/no-wrap inventory:

  • Confirmed page overflow: request value spans in requestRow (View.purs:737-738) inside flex li rows (dist/index.html:200-206).
  • Likely same failure: fact values in factRow (View.purs:776-777) because the value span is not wrapped/truncated.
  • Current long token/root/owner fields mostly wrap because .field-line strong uses overflow-wrap:anywhere (dist/index.html:77-83), but they should still be truncated/copyable rather than wrapped into multi-line blocks.
  • Token rows use overflow-wrap:anywhere (dist/index.html:211-220), so they do not explode the page, but they are not scan-friendly or copyable.
  • Inputs and textareas have no app-level styling; pasted long proof JSON should be contained in a monospace, scrollable proof panel rather than a plain textarea.

docs.title: 3. The MPFS Request/Proof/Retract Model
docs.text:
An MPFS request is a pending on-chain fact operation for a selected token. It is created by a requester and contains:

  • request_id: the request UTxO reference (txid#ix), derived in src/MPFS/Client.purs:539.
  • owner: the requester/owner key hash from the request datum (src/MPFS/Client.purs:532-539).
  • operation: insert, update, or delete, derived from the request datum (src/MPFS/Client.purs:564-573).
  • key, value, fee, and submitted_at (src/MPFS/Client/Types.purs:77-87).

The request set is proof-bearing. The browser preserves the raw /tokens/:id/requests response (src/MPFS/Client.purs:435-459), independently anchors its snapshot root against the second oracle (src/MPFS/App/Verification.purs:163-184), then calls the WASM verifier with op = verify_snapshot (src/MPFS/App/Verification.purs:236-263). The UI should say "Request set verified" and expose proof details: snapshot slot, trusted root, verifier op, verdict, and raw proof/envelope copy.

The request phase is computed from token timing:

  • processable: now - submitted_at <= process_time
  • retractable: after process time, until process_time + retract_time
  • expired: after both windows

That logic is in src/MPFS/App/Facts.purs:148-158. The UI must make authority explicit: the requester can retract during the retract window. Processing belongs to the token/agent path for processable requests; rejecting belongs to expired requests. A row should show both the row's requester and whether the connected wallet is "you", then enable only the actions the connected wallet and phase allow.

docs.title: 4. Redesign Proposal: House Material Style
docs.text:
Keep the first screen as the actual workbench, not a landing page. Use a Material-like app shell, but implement it in Halogen and CSS:

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| MPFS Browser                              Wallet chip | Network | API |
+----------------------------+------------------------------------------+
| Tokens                     | Token 976821db…aaacbc6     Verified chips |
| [Refresh] [Register]       | owner 8da87507…526f0c9f (not you)        |
| [Mine only toggle]         +------------------------------------------+
| > 976821db…aaacbc6  Mine   | Facts                                    |
|   98207724…59a32b Read     | Key        Value              Actions    |
|                            | schema…   7b2261…7d       [edit][delete]|
|                            +------------------------------------------+
|                            | Pending Requests                         |
|                            | [Process selected] [Reject expired]      |
|                            | Op  Key  Value  Requester  Phase Actions |
|                            | Ins cfg  {...}  you        Expired       |
+----------------------------+------------------------------------------+

Concrete components:

  • App shell: top-app-bar, token-sidebar, workspace, section-header, paper, table, status-chip, alert, dialog, icon-button.
  • Theme tokens: copy the visual language from purescript-spa-kit/mui and mpfs-spa: neutral #f7f8f9 background, white paper, primary #255f85, success #2f6f50, warning #b46a1c, 6px radius, dense spacing.
  • Tokens: persistent left rail with selected row, owner chip, "Mine" / "Read-only", refresh/register icons, empty states with next action. Do not require the user to remember to switch tabs after selecting.
  • Facts: table with bounded height and sticky header. Columns: decoded key label, key hash chip, decoded value/summary, value hash chip, proof status, actions. Use dialogs for insert/update/delete instead of three always-visible raw forms.
  • Requests: table on desktop, stacked cards on mobile. Columns: select, operation chip, key, value, requester, age/deadline, phase, proof, actions. The row title should read like "Insert cfg -> ", not raw concatenated text.
  • Request cards on mobile:
    • [Insert] [expired] [request set verified]
Key      7b227479…6669677d  [copy]
Value    7b226167…317d7d    [copy]
Requester 8da87507…526f0c9f (you)
Submitted 2h 14m ago | Process window ended | Retract window ended
Actions: disabled with reason, or Retract when requester + retractable
    • Proof detail: a collapsible drawer/dialog per request set and per fact lookup. Show:
    • verifier verdict chip
    • snapshot slot and root
    • trusted root source
    • verifier operation (verify_snapshot, verify_fact_inclusion, etc.)
    • raw proof/envelope with copy/download
    • failure reason when rejected
    • Hash chip pattern: render full values as front…back, e.g. 7b227479…6669677d. Use monospace text, max-width, overflow:hidden, and a visible copy button. Hover/focus can show a tooltip with the full value; click copies full value. CQuisitor's pattern is the right behavior reference (HashWithTooltip.tsx:17, CopyButton.tsx:11, globals.css:7394, globals.css:8998).
    • Overflow handling:
    • No raw hash should be a bare flex item.
    • Every table cell containing untrusted or user-provided bytes must use min-width:0.
    • Desktop tables may scroll horizontally inside their own container; the page itself should not.
    • Mobile request/fact cards should stack fields and use chips, not tables squeezed below readability.

docs.title: 5. Framework Recommendation
docs.text:
Recommend A: keep Halogen; implement the Material design language in Halogen + CSS.

Rationale:

  • Trust boundary wins for this app. cardano-mpfs-browser is asset-managing and signs/submits wallet transactions. Its current runtime npm tree is one package: @bjorn3/browser_wasi_shim. The redesigned React+MUI mpfs-spa lockfile has 86 runtime packages, including MUI, Emotion, React, and transitive Babel/utility packages.
  • The existing project spec already points this way: specs/32-port-mpfs-spa/spec.md:12-21 says the target architecture is Halogen with a small npm runtime surface and that mpfs-spa is reference behavior only; specs/32-port-mpfs-spa/spec.md:42 explicitly excludes react-basic, MUI, and Emotion.
  • Exact MUI component reuse is not worth increasing the signing-page JS surface. A compromised presentation dependency can alter what the page asks the wallet to sign.
  • Visual consistency does not require importing MUI. The Material language is mostly layout, density, typography, color tokens, elevation/borders, chips, tables, dialogs, and icon-button patterns. Those are straightforward in Halogen/plain CSS.
  • Effort is moderate but bounded. The current UI is centralized in src/MPFS/App/View.purs and one inline CSS block. Rebuilding a small Halogen component kit is less risky than moving the app back to React or embedding React islands.

What to reuse:

  • From purescript-spa-kit/mui: the component vocabulary and theme constants, not the MUI bindings.
  • From cardano-mpfs-offchain-ui-redesign/mpfs-spa: the two-pane workbench, token ownership filtering, owner chips, request/fact tables, phase chips, dialogs, and action gating ideas.
  • From CQuisitor: truncating/copyable hash chips and proof/detail inspection patterns.
  • From cardano-ledger-inspector: Halogen clipboard/action patterns for copied state.

When B would be acceptable:

  • Only for a read-only inspector or demo surface that never requests wallet signatures, or if the organization explicitly relaxes the asset-app npm boundary. For this SPA, B should not be chosen.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Cardano MPFS Browser is the trusted interface between the user and the MPFS protocol. It is the boundary where the digital world (cryptographic proofs, on-chain state, Merkle trees) meets the non-digital world (a human making decisions).

Everything below this layer is verifiable: proofs are mathematical, chain state is consensus, the MPFS service is just a data pipe. But none of that matters if the interface that translates digital facts into human-readable information is wrong. If this code misrepresents a transaction, the user signs something they didn't intend. If it misrenders a fact, the user acts on false data.

This is the trust boundary. This is Web3: not "trustless" in the sense that trust disappears, but that trust is relocated — from opaque servers to auditable client code that verifies proofs before presenting anything to the user.

docs.title: The MPFS Application Pattern
docs.text:
Any application built on MPFS — whether a browser, a CLI, or an automated agent — must follow the same pattern:

  1. Verify — check proofs for every piece of data received from the untrusted service
  2. Interpret — decode raw bytes into domain meaning using a verified schema
  3. Decide — make a trust decision (sign or reject a transaction)

The difference between applications is only in step 3:

  • A browser presents verified facts to a human, who decides
  • An agent applies programmatic logic to verified facts and decides autonomously
  • A CLI does the same as the browser, but in a terminal

The trust architecture is identical. The browser is the reference implementation of this pattern — and the first real MPFS client. Any domain-specific application built on MPFS (a credential verifier, a supply chain tracker, a registry) replicates this same structure, adding domain logic on top of verified facts.

docs.title: MPFS Client Libraries
docs.text:
The verify–interpret–decide machinery is not application-specific. It belongs in a library that any MPFS application can consume. This repository produces two artifacts:

  1. The browser app — the SPA, a consumer of the library
  2. The JS client library — published to npm, usable by any JavaScript/TypeScript application (browser or Node.js)

The library takes the three user inputs (token ID, schema, API URL + institutional root source) and exposes verified facts, decoded transactions, and proof verification. The consumer supplies the "decide" step — a human in the browser, business logic in an agent, a prompt in a CLI.

graph TB
    subgraph "MPFS Client Library"
        IN["Inputs<br/>token ID, schema,<br/>API URL, root source"]
        V["Verify<br/>check proofs"]
        I["Interpret<br/>apply schema"]
        E["Expose<br/>verified data +<br/>decoded transactions"]

        IN --> V --> I --> E
    end

    subgraph "Consumer (the decide step)"
        B["Browser<br/>show to human"]
        A["Agent<br/>apply logic"]
        C["CLI<br/>print to terminal"]
    end

    E --> B
    E --> A
    E --> C

Beyond JavaScript, we are committed to providing the same trust machinery as native libraries for backend and systems integration:

Library Language Target JS/npm PureScript → JS Browser, Node.js Native (C ABI) Haskell or Rust C, C++, Python, Go, any FFI

The native library exposes the same verify–interpret–decide interface via C-compatible FFI, enabling MPFS applications in any language that can call C functions.

docs.title: This Application
docs.text:
The browser serves two purposes:

  1. Fact Explorer — given an MPFS token, query its facts and render them using a verified schema, with full proof verification at every step
  2. MPFS Client — interact with the cage protocol (insert, delete, update) and sign transactions via a CIP-30 wallet, with every unsigned transaction decoded and displayed in human-readable MPFS semantics before signing

docs.title: System Context
docs.text:
graph TB
    subgraph "Trusted"
        User["Human User"]
        Browser["MPFS Browser<br/>(this application)"]
        Wallet["CIP-30 Wallet<br/>(Nami, Eternl, Lace)"]
    end

    subgraph "Untrusted"
        API["MPFS Off-Chain API<br/>(data pipe)"]
        Node["Cardano Node<br/>(behind API)"]
    end

    subgraph "Trust Anchors"
        Oracle["Oracle<br/>(publishes token ID +<br/>schema)"]
        Inst["Institutional Party<br/>(publishes UTXO<br/>Merkle root)"]
    end

    Oracle -->|"token ID + schema"| User
    Inst -->|"UTXO root"| Browser
    User <-->|"view facts,<br/>approve txs"| Browser
    Browser <-->|"query facts,<br/>get proofs,<br/>build txs"| API
    Browser <-->|"sign txs"| Wallet
    API <--> Node

docs.title: What the User Needs
docs.text:
To use the application, a user provides exactly three inputs:

  1. Token ID — published by the oracle (token owner) alongside the schema. The oracle is responsible for making this public.
  2. MPFS API URL — the address of any MPFS off-chain service. This is untrusted — it is just a data pipe.
  3. Institutional UTXO Merkle root source — a trusted party (e.g. Cardano Foundation) that publishes the current UTXO Merkle tree root.

Everything else is provable. The MPFS service is obligated to provide proofs for anything it claims — if it lies or withholds data, the proofs won't verify and the user knows immediately.

docs.title: The Oracle's Responsibility
docs.text:
The oracle (token owner) publishes a configuration document:

{
  "tokenId": "21c5...",
  "schemas": [
    { "format": "cddl", "document": "..." },
    { "format": "json-schema", "document": "..." }
  ]
}
  • The token ID — identifies the cage on-chain
  • The schemas — one or more schema documents with their format, used to decode facts

By publishing the token ID and schemas, the oracle gives users the entry point to independently verify and interpret everything.

docs.title: The Verification Chain
docs.text:
The application verifies facts through a four-layer chain, where each layer is independently provable:

graph LR
    IR["Institutional Root<br/>(trusted anchor)"]
    CP["CSMT Proof<br/>(UTxO existence)"]
    CU["Cage UTxO<br/>(on-chain state)"]
    MP["MPF Proof<br/>(trie inclusion)"]
    F["Fact<br/>(key-value)"]

    IR -- "root matches?" --> CP
    CP -- "UTxO exists?" --> CU
    CU -- "trie root" --> MP
    MP -- "fact exists?" --> F
Layer What it proves Trust source Institutional Root The UTXO Merkle root is authentic Published by a known party (e.g. Cardano Foundation) CSMT Proof The cage UTxO exists in the UTXO set Verified against institutional root Cage UTxO The cage's current trie root Proved to exist on-chain MPF Proof A fact exists in the cage's trie Verified against cage's trie root

No Cardano node is required. The entire chain is verified client-side using cryptographic proofs and a single trusted root.

docs.title: What the User Trusts
docs.text:
• The oracle's published token ID (explicit, public)
  • The institutional root publisher (explicit, auditable)
  • The browser (runs the verification code)
  • Nothing else — not the MPFS off-chain service, not the API

docs.title: The MPFS Service Obligation
docs.text:
The off-chain service is untrusted but has a clear contract: for any data it holds that is committed to the Merkle tree, it must provide the corresponding proof. The user can always verify:

  • Is this fact actually in the trie? (MPF proof)
  • Does this trie root match what's on-chain? (cage UTxO)
  • Does this cage UTxO actually exist? (CSMT proof)
  • Is the UTXO set root authentic? (institutional root)

If any link breaks, the user sees it. The service cannot selectively lie — it either provides valid proofs or the verification fails visibly.

docs.title: Self-Describing Facts
docs.text:
MPFS stores facts as raw bytestrings in the trie. The trie is format-agnostic — it stores whatever bytes the oracle inserts. To enable generic rendering, facts follow a convention: the first 32 bytes of the value are the blake2b-256 hash of the schema document used to encode the rest.

value = schema_hash (32 bytes) ++ payload

The schema hash links the fact to a specific schema document published by the oracle. The browser computes the hash of each known schema and matches it against the prefix. Facts with unknown schema hashes are displayed as raw hex.

This is a convention, not enforced on-chain. The schema hash prefix is what makes facts interpretable by generic clients.

docs.title: Schema Matching
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant O as Oracle
    participant B as Browser
    participant API as MPFS API

    Note over O: Publishes: oracle config<br/>(token ID + schemas)

    B->>B: Receive oracle config
    B->>B: Hash each schema document

    B->>API: GET /tokens/:id/facts/:key
    API-->>B: value bytes + MPF proof

    B->>B: Verify MPF proof
    B->>B: Extract first 32 bytes of value
    B->>B: Match against known schema hashes

    alt Known schema
        B->>B: Decode payload with schema
        B->>B: Render structured data
    else Unknown schema
        B->>B: Render as hex
    end

docs.title: Schema Formats
docs.text:
The schema format is extensible. The format field in the oracle config determines how the browser decodes the payload after the 32-byte hash prefix:

Format Schema language Payload encoding cddl CDDL (RFC 8610) CBOR json-schema JSON Schema JSON (UTF-8)

CDDL schemas are embedded as strings in the oracle config JSON. The document field is the hash source — blake2b(document_string) must match the 32-byte prefix in fact values.

New formats can be added without protocol changes — just a new decoder and a schema document from the oracle.

docs.title: Key and Value Structure
docs.text:
For a given schema, both the key and the value payload (bytes after the 32-byte hash prefix) must conform to the schema. The schema describes the structure of both.

For example, a CDDL schema for the moog test-run application:

fact-key = {
  type: "test-run",
  platform: tstr,
  repository: {
    organization: tstr,
    repo: tstr
  },
  commitId: tstr,
  try: uint,
  requester: tstr
}

fact-value = {
  phase: "pending" / "accepted"
        / "finished" / "rejected",
  duration: uint,
  ? outcome: "success" / "failure" / "unknown",
  ? url: tstr,
  ? from: fact-value
}

docs.title: Multiple Schemas
docs.text:
A token can accumulate multiple schemas over time. The oracle may update the encoding format, add new fact types, or evolve the data structure. Each schema version is a separate document with a distinct hash.

Old facts remain readable because old schemas remain in the oracle config. The browser matches each fact's schema hash against all known schemas. Schemas should never be removed from the oracle config — removing a schema makes older facts unreadable by generic clients.

docs.title: Transaction Flow
docs.text:
The client interacts with the cage protocol through the MPFS API. The API builds unsigned transactions; the client decodes them, displays their MPFS semantics in human-readable form, and delegates signing to the user's CIP-30 wallet.

Because the API is untrusted, the client always decodes the unsigned CBOR before requesting a signature — the user sees exactly what they are signing.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant FE as Frontend
    participant API as MPFS API
    participant W as CIP-30 Wallet

    U->>FE: "Insert fact X=Y into token T"
    FE->>API: POST /tx/request/insert {token, key, value, address}
    API-->>FE: unsigned tx (CBOR hex)

    FE->>FE: Decode CBOR, extract TxIns

    loop For each TxIn
        FE->>API: GET /utxo/:txin
        API-->>FE: TxOut (datum, value, address)
        FE->>API: GET /utxo/:txin/proof
        API-->>FE: CSMT inclusion proof
        FE->>FE: Verify TxIn exists in UTXO set
    end

    FE->>FE: Parse MPFS semantics from tx body
    FE->>FE: Render resolved inputs with proof status

    FE->>U: Display verified transaction
    Note over FE,U: Inputs (verified on-chain):<br/>• Cage UTxO root=abc... ✓<br/>Operation:<br/>• Insert key "X" = value "Y"<br/>• Fee: 1.5 ADA

    U->>FE: "Approve"
    FE->>W: api.signTx(unsignedTx)
    W-->>FE: signed tx

    FE->>API: POST /tx/submit {signed tx}
    API-->>FE: TxId
    FE->>U: "Submitted: tx abc123..."

docs.title: Input Resolution and Verification
docs.text:
The unsigned transaction contains TxIns — references to UTxOs being spent. Raw TxIns are opaque hashes. The client resolves each TxIn to its full TxOut content and verifies it exists in the UTXO set via a CSMT proof.

graph LR
    subgraph "Unsigned Tx"
        TI1["TxIn #1<br/>(hash)"]
        TI2["TxIn #2<br/>(hash)"]
    end

    subgraph "Resolved + Verified"
        TO1["TxOut #1<br/>cage UTxO<br/>root: abc...<br/>value: 5 ADA<br/>✓ CSMT proof"]
        TO2["TxOut #2<br/>user UTxO<br/>addr: addr1...<br/>value: 10 ADA<br/>✓ CSMT proof"]
    end

    TI1 -->|"GET /utxo/:txin<br/>+ proof"| TO1
    TI2 -->|"GET /utxo/:txin<br/>+ proof"| TO2

This is critical: without resolving and verifying inputs, the user cannot know what the transaction actually spends. The API could claim a TxIn points to one UTxO while the transaction actually consumes another. The CSMT proof makes this impossible — each input is independently proven to exist in the UTXO set.

docs.title: What the Frontend Displays
docs.text:
From the decoded transaction and resolved inputs, the frontend presents:

Field Source Display Inputs TxIns, resolved via API Full TxOut content with CSMT proof status Cage UTxO Input datum Trie root, owner, config — verified on-chain Operation Redeemer (Contribute/Modify/Mint) "Insert", "Delete", "Update", "Boot", "Retract", "End" Token Asset name in tx outputs Token identifier Key Request datum field Decoded via verified schema Value Request datum field Decoded via verified schema Fee Tx fee field ADA amount Address Tx output addresses Bech32, highlighted if user's

If the schema is verified, the key and value are rendered in structured form. Otherwise they are shown as hex with a warning that no verified schema is available.

Every input carries a proof indicator. If any input cannot be verified, the UI warns prominently — the user should not sign a transaction with unverified inputs.

docs.title: Transaction Signing State Machine
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SelectOperation: user chooses action
    SelectOperation --> BuildingTx: submit parameters
    BuildingTx --> TxReceived: API returns unsigned CBOR

    TxReceived --> Decoding: parse CBOR
    Decoding --> Decoded: extract MPFS semantics
    Decoding --> DecodeFailed: malformed or unexpected

    Decoded --> ReviewPending: display to user
    ReviewPending --> Approved: user approves
    ReviewPending --> Rejected: user rejects

    Approved --> Signing: CIP-30 signTx
    Signing --> Signed: wallet returns signature
    Signing --> SignFailed: wallet refused

    Signed --> Submitting: POST /tx/submit
    Submitting --> Submitted: TxId received
    Submitting --> SubmitFailed: submission error

    Rejected --> [*]
    DecodeFailed --> [*]
    SignFailed --> [*]
    SubmitFailed --> [*]
    Submitted --> [*]

docs.title: Why the Server Doesn't Matter
docs.text:
The MPFS off-chain service is a convenience layer. The client independently verifies everything:

  • Facts — verified via the full proof chain
  • Transactions — decoded and displayed before signing
  • State — anchored on-chain via cage UTxOs

The server could lie, omit data, or be compromised. The client catches it because every claim requires a cryptographic proof. This is the key value proposition: a trusted client that works with any untrusted server.

docs.title: Connection Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant FE as Frontend
    participant W as CIP-30 Wallet

    FE->>FE: Detect window.cardano.*
    FE->>U: Show available wallets (Nami, Eternl, Lace...)

    U->>FE: Select wallet
    FE->>W: cardano.nami.enable()
    W-->>FE: API handle

    FE->>W: api.getUsedAddresses()
    W-->>FE: [addr1, addr2, ...]
    FE->>FE: Store primary address (hex)

docs.title: API Surface Used
docs.text:
CIP-30 Method Purpose cardano.<wallet>.enable() Connect to wallet api.getUsedAddresses() Get user's address for tx building api.signTx(tx, partialSign) Sign unsigned transaction api.getNetworkId() Verify correct network (mainnet/testnet)

The frontend does not use api.submitTx() — submission goes through the MPFS API which handles chain submission via its node connection.

docs.title: State Persistence
docs.text: The entire application state is serialized to localStorage. If the browser tab closes — accidentally or intentionally — reopening restores the exact same view: same token, same fact, same pending transaction, same wallet connection.

docs.title: What Lives Where
docs.text: Storage Content Purpose URL hash Navigation: token, fact key, current page Bookmarkable, shareable localStorage Session config: API URL, root source, connected wallet, verified schemas, view state Survives tab close

docs.title: URL Structure
docs.text:
#/token/abc123                    → token detail
#/token/abc123/facts              → fact list
#/token/abc123/facts/mykey        → fact detail + proof
#/token/abc123/tx/insert          → build insert tx

docs.title: Recovery Guarantee
docs.text:
The app serializes its full state to localStorage on every state change. On load, it reads localStorage first, then the URL hash. The result: Ctrl+W → reopen → identical view. No re-entry of API URL, no wallet reconnection prompt, no lost context.

This is critical for the trust boundary role: the user must always be able to see where they are in a verification or signing flow, even after an interruption.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
graph TB
    subgraph "Fact Explorer"
        TL["Token List<br/>All known MPFS tokens"]
        TD["Token Detail<br/>State, root, config"]
        FL["Fact List<br/>All facts in token"]
        FD["Fact Detail<br/>Decoded value + proof status"]
    end

    subgraph "MPFS Client"
        TX["Build Transaction<br/>Select operation"]
        TV["Review Transaction<br/>Decoded MPFS semantics"]
        TS["Sign & Submit<br/>CIP-30 wallet"]
    end

    subgraph "Proof Inspector"
        PI["Proof Chain<br/>Full verification status"]
    end

    TL --> TD --> FL --> FD
    TD --> TX --> TV --> TS
    FD --> PI

docs.title: Token List View
docs.text:
Shows all MPFS tokens the API tracks:

  • Token ID (asset name, hex + decoded if UTF-8)
  • Owner (payment key hash → bech32 if possible)
  • Current root (truncated hash)
  • Pending requests count
  • Phase indicator (process/retract window)

docs.title: Fact Detail View
docs.text:
For a single fact:

  • Key — raw hex + schema-decoded rendering
  • Value — raw hex + schema-decoded rendering
  • Proof status:
    • ✓ MPF proof valid against cage root
    • ✓ Cage UTxO exists (CSMT proof valid)
    • ✓ CSMT root matches institutional publisher
    • Or: ⚠ partial verification (e.g. no institutional root configured)

docs.title: Proof Inspector
docs.text:
Expandable panel showing the full verification chain:

  • Institutional root source and value
  • CSMT proof steps (Merkle path)
  • Cage UTxO details (TxIn, datum, value)
  • MPF proof steps (trie path)
  • Final verdict: fully verified / partially verified / unverified

docs.title: Fact Verification State Machine
docs.text:
Each fact goes through a verification pipeline. The UI reflects the current state with visual indicators:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Fetching: query fact
    Fetching --> ProofReceived: API returns bytes + proof

    ProofReceived --> MPFValid: MPF proof valid
    ProofReceived --> MPFFailed: MPF proof invalid

    MPFValid --> CageVerified: cage UTxO exists (CSMT proof)
    MPFValid --> CageUnverified: no CSMT proof available

    CageVerified --> FullyVerified: root matches institutional
    CageVerified --> PartiallyVerified: no institutional root

    CageUnverified --> PartiallyVerified

    FullyVerified --> [*]
    PartiallyVerified --> [*]
    MPFFailed --> [*]
State UI Indicator Meaning Fetching Spinner Awaiting API response MPF Failed Red Fact proof invalid — data cannot be trusted Partially Verified Yellow Fact is in trie, but chain anchor incomplete Fully Verified Green Complete proof chain from fact to institutional root

docs.title: Institutional Root Sources
docs.text:
The application needs at least one trusted source for the UTXO Merkle root. This is configurable:

  • URL endpoint — the institutional party publishes the current root at a known URL (simplest)
  • On-chain reference — the root is published in a datum on-chain (self-referential but removes the URL dependency)
  • Multiple sources — cross-reference roots from multiple publishers for higher confidence

The UI shows which root source is active and when it was last updated.

docs.title: API Dependency
docs.text: The frontend consumes the MPFS off-chain HTTP API. Current endpoint status:

docs.title: Available (PR #108)
docs.text: Endpoint Purpose GET /status Service health and sync status GET /tokens List all tracked tokens GET /tokens/:id Token state (owner, root, config) GET /tokens/:id/root Current trie root GET /tokens/:id/facts/:key Fact value + MPF proof GET /tokens/:id/proofs/:key MPF proof only GET /tokens/:id/requests Pending requests POST /tx/boot Build boot transaction POST /tx/request/insert Build insert request tx POST /tx/request/delete Build delete request tx POST /tx/update Build update tx POST /tx/retract Build retract tx POST /tx/end Build end tx POST /tx/submit Submit signed tx

docs.title: Needed (issue #117)
docs.text: Endpoint Purpose GET /utxo/:txin Resolve TxIn to full UTxO GET /utxo/:txin/proof CSMT inclusion proof GET /csmt/root Current UTXO Merkle root

docs.title: Technology Stack
docs.text:
• PureScript with Halogen (component framework)
  • Nix flake for reproducible dev environment
  • esbuild for bundling (via spago)
  • MkDocs with Material theme for documentation
  • No backend — static SPA served from GitHub Pages or alongside the MPFS API

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
1. CBOR decoding in PureScript — which library? FFI to a JS CBOR library? How much of the Cardano tx structure do we need to parse?
  2. Institutional root protocol — is there a standard for publishing UTXO Merkle roots, or do we define one?
  3. Multi-token view — should the explorer support comparing facts across tokens, or is it strictly per-token?

docs.title: MPFS Browser — design source of truth
docs.text:
SPEC.md is the authoritative UI/UX spec for the MPFS Browser workbench, produced from the design brief. The clean-sheet Halogen build implements it screen by screen.

  • SPEC.md — tokens, layout, screens, components (with states), interactions, Halogen-port notes.
  • MPFS Browser.dc.html — interactive mockup (dc-runtime; the <x-dc> block is the design markup).
  • HashChip.dc.html — the reusable copy-chip component.

Build target: match this design in Halogen + plain CSS (no React/MUI runtime); re-score with tools/ux-judge.

docs.title: MPFS Browser — Design Specification
docs.text:
A web workbench for inspecting on-chain MPFS (Merkle Patricia Forest Store) data and its cryptographic verification, and for submitting changes with a CIP-30 wallet.

Built as a Material-3-flavored, hand-rolled component set in plain HTML/CSS so it ports directly to PureScript/Halogen (no React/MUI/Tailwind runtime).

  • Entry point: MPFS Browser.dc.html
  • Reusable component: HashChip.dc.html (copyable, middle-truncated identifier)

docs.title: 1. Product principles
docs.text:
1. Data + its verification is the star. Everything secondary (network, wallet, endpoint) is demoted to the chrome.
  2. Read without a wallet. Tokens, facts, requests, and proofs are fully browsable with no wallet. A wallet gates only submit and retract.
  3. No raw hex walls. Every long identifier is a copyable, middle-truncated chip (xxxx…yyyy). Fact keys/values are shown decoded to UTF-8 JSON.
  4. Signing is deliberate. Writes always route through a decoded intent review before the wallet prompt.
  5. No page-level horizontal overflow at any width. Long bytes live in bounded chips; tables scroll inside their own container only.

docs.title: Spacing scale
docs.text: 2 · 4 · 6 · 8 · 10 · 12 · 14 · 16 · 20 · 24 · 32 px. Dense by default; card padding 12–18px, table cell padding 9–14px.

docs.title: Radius
docs.text:
• Chips / inputs / buttons / cards: 6px
  • Pills (verdict, phase, network): 12–20px (fully rounded)
  • Avatars / status dots: 50%

docs.title: Type scale (Roboto / Roboto Mono)
docs.text: Token Size / weight Usage display 20px / 700 Page title ("Token") title 17px / 700 Verdict card heading subtitle 15px / 500 Metric values body 13px / 400 Table cells, controls label 12px / 500 Secondary labels caption 11px / 400 Deadlines, hints overline 11px / 600, .5px, uppercase Column headers, metric labels mono Roboto Mono 12–13px All hashes, JSON, slots

docs.title: Elevation
docs.text:
• Level 0: borders only (1px solid outline) — the default for cards/tables.
  • Level 1: 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.25) — toggle knob, floating chips.
  • Drawer/dialog scrim: rgba(20,23,28,.45) + panel shadow 0 8px 32px rgba(0,0,0,.24).

docs.title: 3. Layout
docs.text:
Desktop (1440): sticky app bar → two-column grid 300px | 1fr. - Left token sidebar: search, "Owned by me" toggle, scrollable token list (each row: kind dot, xxxx…yyyy id, MINE badge, facts + pending counts). - Right workspace: token header (id chip, owner chip, verdict pill) → 4-up summary strip (state root, max fee, process window, retract window) → tab bar (Facts / Pending / Verification) → active panel. Max content width 1160px.

Tablet (768): sidebar narrows; summary strip wraps to 2-up; tables keep their own horizontal scroll container.

Mobile (390): sidebar collapses to a token picker pinned on top; workspace stacks single-column; Pending rows render as stacked cards instead of a table; summary strip becomes a 2-col grid.

docs.title: 4. Screens & journeys
docs.text:
1. First run / connect — read-only browsing is live immediately. A single explanatory banner states what MPFS Browser does and that a wallet is only for writes. No dead-ends; "Connect wallet" is available but never blocking.
  2. Tokens (registry) — scannable sidebar list; search by id/owner; "Mine" filter; selecting a token loads its workspace inline (no route change feel).
  3. Facts — bounded, scrollable table. Each row: decoded key label + copyable key JSON well, decoded value JSON well (scrolls if tall), inclusion proof chip, row actions (Proof, Edit-if-mine). Dimmed empty state when the forest is empty.
  4. Pending requests — table (desktop) / cards (mobile). Each row: op chip (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), decoded key→value, requester chip + YOU badge, age, fee, phase chip (Processable → Retractable → Expired), proof chip, and a Retract action gated by phase + authority.
  5. Verification / proof inspector — persistent verdict card listing the three checks (second-oracle agreement, facts-set completeness, per-fact inclusion proofs) with snapshot slot, trusted root, verifier op; a proof drawer opens per-fact and per-set with raw proof (copy/download) and a failure reason on reject.
  6. Write dialogs + intent review — insert/update/delete/retract in a dialog: edit → decoded "what you're about to sign" review → sign (CIP-30) → done.

docs.title: 5. Component inventory (states)
docs.text: Component States Button (primary / outline / text / danger) default · hover · focus · disabled (with reason) · loading (spinner) Hash chip + copy default · hover · copied (✓, 1.2s) — xxxx…yyyy, optional label Status / phase chip processable (blue) · retractable (amber) · expired (neutral) · verified (green) · pending (amber) Op chip insert (green) · update (blue) · delete (red) Data table header · row · row-hover · empty (dimmed, iconographic) · own-scroll container Text field default · focus (primary ring) · with JSON validation error Toggle on (primary) · off (neutral), knob elevation 1 Verdict card pass (green) · reject (red, with reason) — check list with PASS/FAIL badges Proof drawer scrim + slide-in panel; copy / download raw proof; failure reason Dialog connect-gate · edit · review (decoded intent) · signing (spinner) · done Sidebar item default · hover · active (primary container + border) Alert / banner info (read-only notice) · warning (request lifecycle)

docs.title: 6. Interaction notes
docs.text:
• Token select: clicking a sidebar row sets the active token, resets to the Facts tab, and closes any open drawer. Active row uses primary-container fill + border; kind dot turns primary.
  • Request action gating: Retract is enabled only when phase === 'retractable' and the connected wallet is the original requester. When disabled, the button is visibly inert and shows the exact reason beneath it ("Only the requester may retract" / "Retract opens after the process window" / "Retract window has closed"). Retract itself routes through the review→sign flow.
  • Proof access: proof chips and Proof buttons open the drawer scoped to that fact/request; the workspace verdict pill opens the set-level proof.
  • Write → review → sign: if no wallet, the dialog first shows a connect step. After editing, the review step renders the decoded key/value and computed intent; only then does "Sign" trigger the (simulated) CIP-30 prompt → signing spinner → done confirmation.
  • Empty / loading / error: tables show dimmed iconographic empty states; verification supports a reject verdict (red card + failure reason); disabled controls always explain themselves.
  • Copy feedback: hash chips swap the copy glyph for a green ✓ for 1.2s.

docs.title: 7. Implementation notes (Halogen port)
docs.text:
• All styling is inline / token-driven — map tokens to a Halogen theme record and swap the light/dark table above.
  • HashChip is the one genuinely reusable widget; everything else is composed from the token + chip + table primitives.
  • No component depends on a JS runtime library; interactions (tab switch, token select, drawer, dialog steps) are plain state transitions.
  • Tables own their horizontal scroll (overflow-x:auto, min-width on <table>) so the page never overflows.

docs.title: 8. Status of this deliverable
docs.text:
Implemented interactively in MPFS Browser.dc.html: - Token sidebar (search, Mine filter, select) · token summary + verdict pill - Facts table with decoded JSON + inclusion proof chips - Pending requests table with op/requester/YOU/age/fee/phase/deadline and fully gated Retract - Verification tab: verdict card + three checks + snapshot / root / verifier op

Documented above and scaffolded for build-out: proof drawer, write/review/sign dialogs, first-run view, and 390/768 responsive frames.
